title: The king and the meal
hook: Narada knew every Veda and was still hungry; the sutras answer with a king and a meal
carry: bhakti is lived, not just known

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: love is the fruit, not only the road, and the Lord is fond of humility, empty hands.

Year two met Narada in the Chandogya Upanishad, sitting before the sage Sanatkumara with a whole library in his head: all four Vedas, the old stories, grammar, mathematics, the stars. Then he said the honest sentence. Sir, I know the sacred texts, but I do not know the Self. And I am in sorrow. Take me across. Hold on to that scene, because today the Narada Bhakti Sutras ask the same question about love. If love is above the other roads, how do you get it? Isn't knowledge the way in?
screen: `NARADA KNOWS EVERYTHING.` → `AND IS STILL IN SORROW.` → `ISN'T KNOWLEDGE THE WAY IN?`

segments.voice: The sutras answer the way they did on the marks of love in year two: they let several voices speak. Some say, the text reports, that knowledge alone is the means to bhakti: you have to know who the Lord is before you can love him. Others say knowledge and love depend on each other: picture two cards propped into a little tent. Then a third voice, the sons of Brahma, whom commentators take to be Sanatkumara and his brothers, the ever-young sages of the Puranas. Sanatkumara: the same teacher who heard Narada admit his learning hadn't freed him. They say bhakti is its own fruit, not produced by something else. Here the sutras side with them, and give their evidence: a king, a house, and a meal. Knowing about a king doesn't make the king pleased with you. Knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger. So, the sutras conclude, those who long for freedom should take up love itself. Notice what they don't say. Not that knowledge is bad, or that you should stop learning. Narada was a great scholar. The sutras just refuse to let knowing about stand in for the thing. That's why devotional Hindus don't stop at reading. They sing the names, offer the lamp, stand for darshan, take prasad. The scripture tells you about the meal; worship is where you eat. The king has to be met. The meal has to be eaten.
screen: `SOME SAY: KNOWLEDGE IS THE MEANS.` · `THE SONS OF BRAHMA: ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `WORSHIP IS WHERE YOU EAT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you love and notice, for a few breaths, how much you know about them: their habits, their history, the facts. Then let the facts go quiet and simply be near them, the way you'd sit beside someone without needing to talk. If you pray, you can do this with God, setting aside what you know about God for a while.
Bhakti. For the sutras, its own fruit: knowing about the king doesn't please him, and knowing about the meal doesn't feed you.
Your line: bhakti is lived, not just known. Knowing about the meal isn't eating it. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1215 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE COMPANY OF GREAT SOULS.`

howItsDone: Teachers of the Narada Bhakti Sutras use the king and the meal to explain that devotion is something lived, not only studied, and pair the study of the text with worship, singing and service.

fork.setup: three views on how love is reached are set before you. which one do the sutras themselves side with?
options: knowledge and love depend on each other.
fork.reveal: they side with the sons of Brahma: love is its own fruit. knowing about a king doesn't please him, and knowing about a meal doesn't end hunger.

original.note: Sanskrit phala, fruit: the sutras call bhakti svayam phala-rūpā, of the form of its own fruit.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you learn enough about God, love will follow.

what a scholar hears: tasyā jñānam eva sādhanam ity eke, then anyonyāśrayatvam ity anye, then svayaṃ phala-rūpateti brahma-kumārāḥ: three views set side by side, and the text sides with the third.

chat.says: Sam asked why Nani still goes to bhajans every week when she knows the whole Gita by heart. wait, why does she?
options: the sutras say knowing about a meal doesn't feed you. bhakti has to be lived: sung, offered, done.
she doesn't need to. once you know the scripture, worship is optional.
it's just a social thing. it isn't really about God.
chat.meaning: The sutras side with the sons of Brahma: bhakti is its own fruit. Knowing about a king or a meal isn't being welcomed or fed, so devotees keep singing and worshipping.

tie.story: Narada knew every Veda and still sat before Sanatkumara in sorrow, and his sutras say knowing about a meal never ended anyone's hunger.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam that Nani isn't just studying God at bhajan night; she's coming to the meal.
tie.you: what do you know all about but haven't tasted yet?

Brahma.meaning: the creator god, whose sons are ever-young sages

Chandogya Upanishad.meaning: an ancient Upanishad where Narada comes to a teacher

Puranas.meaning: ancient books of stories of gods and sages

Narada.meaning: the sage to whom the sutras are attributed

Sanatkumara.meaning: an ever-young sage, a son of Brahma, who taught Narada

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 28–33 (knowledge as means; mutual dependence; the sons of Brahma: its own fruit; the king, the house, the meal; so take up bhakti)

notes: Sutras 28–33 paraphrased. Sutra 31 names a king, a house and a meal; sutra 32 spells out only the king (not pleased) and hunger (not satisfied).
